Adopted Ordinance No. 1040 on 16 July 2024 and introduced it on 18 June 2024, both 5-0, and is named in the ordinance’s own roll call. The ordinance repeals and re-enacts Corte Madera Municipal Code chapters 15.08 and 15.13 as a Single-Family Building Remodel Energy Reach Code that the Town Council finds to be more stringent than the State energy standards: a Covered Project must reach a Target Score drawn from a measure menu of heat-pump water and space heaters, induction cooktops with the gas lines capped, and solar PV, with Electric Readiness mandatory for certain scopes, and it requires enhanced electric-vehicle charging infrastructure in new construction. The recitals tie those requirements to the Town’s 2020 Climate Action Plan goal of cutting greenhouse gases to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030 and to the climate emergency the Council declared on 1 December 2020. That is chair 1 — a required shift to clean energy through mandates and a firm deadline. It is not chair 2: the ordinance offers no subsidy, tax credit or public investment. It is not chair 3: it does nothing about permitting or the grid. The companion Ordinance No. 1039, adopted the same night by the same 5-0 vote, repeals the Town’s all-electric new-construction chapter — but its own recitals give the reason as the Ninth Circuit’s holding in California Restaurant Association v. City of Berkeley that such mandates are preempted by the federal Energy Policy and Conservation Act, final once rehearing en banc was denied on 2 January 2024, and state that the repeal is to avoid likely litigation. Read together the two ordinances are a town replacing a preempted mandate with the strongest one still lawfully available to it, not retreating from mandates.

Adopted Ordinance No. 1040 on 16 July 2024 and introduced it on 18 June 2024, both 5-0, and is named in the ordinance’s own roll call. The ordinance repeals and re-enacts Corte Madera Municipal Code chapters 15.08 and 15.13 as a Single-Family Building Remodel Energy Reach Code that the Town Council finds to be more stringent than the State energy standards: a Covered Project must reach a Target Score drawn from a measure menu of heat-pump water and space heaters, induction cooktops with the gas lines capped, and solar PV, with Electric Readiness mandatory for certain scopes, and it requires enhanced electric-vehicle charging infrastructure in new construction. The recitals tie those requirements to the Town’s 2020 Climate Action Plan goal of cutting greenhouse gases to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030 and to the climate emergency the Council declared on 1 December 2020. That is chair 1 — a required shift to clean energy through mandates and a firm deadline. It is not chair 2: the ordinance offers no subsidy, tax credit or public investment. It is not chair 3: it does nothing about permitting or the grid. The companion Ordinance No. 1039, adopted the same night by the same 5-0 vote, repeals the Town’s all-electric new-construction chapter — but its own recitals give the reason as the Ninth Circuit’s holding in California Restaurant Association v. City of Berkeley that such mandates are preempted by the federal Energy Policy and Conservation Act, final once rehearing en banc was denied on 2 January 2024, and state that the repeal is to avoid likely litigation. Read together the two ordinances are a town replacing a preempted mandate with the strongest one still lawfully available to it, not retreating from mandates.
